You asked if people like their jobs. I like mine. I'm a mechanical designer, and a good one. I like doing my work, and I think if most people knew the truth, they'd be glad I do it. I do well at my job because I have to. Because the work has to be right. It has to be right, or people die. I'm a fallible human being, but I know I'm fallible, which is why I am particularly, studiously cautious and thorough with my work. I'm NOT confident, and that is my strength. Now compare that to an AI doing my job. An Ai will usually be right, but maybe 5-10% of the time, it will not only be wrong, but confidently wrong. Drastically wrong in ways humans can't even anticipate. I've had junior engineers work under me, and they make mistakes. but they're human mistakes. A human will miss a dimension, or have a typo in a BOM, or transpose numbers, or get a measurement incorrect on a part and it doesn't fit the assembly, etc. These are human mistakes. Junior engineers are more prone to these, which is why we look out for these errors and catch them. A human will NOT, however, decided to connect two parts together with a hamburger instead of a bolt, or make a part out of 2 dimensional planes with nothing inside, because an AI can and will do those things. AI can be wrong in ways we can't even think of - why is why AI, as it is, can't come anywhere near being able to mechanically design things, it has no intuition, it does not understand geometry, or space, or the real world. Good design isn't about making things perfect, it's about making things that will function perfectly, despite having been imperfectly manufactured, on imperfect tools, by imperfect people, built in an imperfect process, and installed in an imperfect environment. No manufactured part has ever, or will ever be perfect. Ever. An AI cannot experience ANY of the real world, and as such, cannot possibly anticipate the imperfect variances that are literally unavoidable, and predictable.... at least, to a being that happens to live in the real world.

I have over 25 years of experience. Early in my career, I became a "Sr. QA Manager" at a startup. From 1998 - 2001, I ascended the ladder by qutting a job and getting a major raise with promotion at a new job. I went from entry-level to Manager in just three years. But it all crashed with the "Dot Com" bubble of 2001. That was a major recession of the early 2000s. The job market was so bad I wound up working construction labor while searching for a new job. I felt like "Peter" in "Office Space" at the very end when he is doing construction digging labor. I did that in Denver. From that experience, I found that I just prefer consulting. I have been working on master's degrees over the years and am now have six. Currently, I work on a PhD to study AI while doing full time consulting. I hope to get into R&D later after this PhD ends. I think the IT corporate ladder is scary with the offshore model, layoffs, instability, tariffs, etc. I have seen some really bad politics with power grabs in my time. I can tell horror stories all day about it. Consulting keeps things brief with the option to leave if it gets like that.
